name: Halesi Mahadev and Maratika Caves
tagline: Cave shrine sacred to Shiva devotees, Buddhists and the Kirat Rai
meta_description: Halesi Mahadev (Maratika Caves) guide: Khotang cave temple sacred to Hindus, Buddhists and Kirat, road from Kathmandu, helicopter yatra, Shivaratri, stays.
summary: Halesi Mahadev, also called the Maratika Caves, is a limestone cave temple near Mahadevsthan village in Khotang district, sacred to Hindus as a home of Shiva, to Buddhists as the place Guru Rinpoche attained long-life realisation, and to the Kirat Rai as an ancestral site. It is about 9–10 hours by road or 45 minutes by helicopter from Kathmandu.
intro: The Halesi caves open into a hillside above the Dudh Koshi and Sun Koshi valleys in Khotang district, between roughly 950 and 1,450 m. The main cave has a wide, half-moon entrance facing east and a domed chamber about 60 m across, lit by a hole in the roof. Hindu pilgrims come to worship Halesi Mahadev, a form of Shiva, at the natural lingam inside, and legend says Shiva hid here from the demon Bhasmasur. Smaller caves nearby are linked to Parvati and other deities.

For Tibetan Buddhists this is Maratika, the cave where Guru Padmasambhava and his consort Mandarava are said to have practised and attained the realisation of long life in the 8th century. Monasteries built since the 1980s stand around the site, and Buddhist pilgrims, including many from Bhutan, Sikkim and abroad, come for long-life retreats. The Kirat Rai of the area regard Halesi as the dwelling place of an ancestor and worship it in their own rites.

Halesi is a long road journey from Kathmandu, about 230 km on the BP Highway via Sindhuli and then hill roads through Ghurmi and the Sun Koshi valley, taking 9–10 hours. Helicopters cover it in about 45 minutes. The biggest crowds come on Maha Shivaratri in February or March, and also around Bala Chaturdashi and in the Hindu month of Shrawan. Visiting is easy for most ages: the caves involve steps and some low passages, but no long walking.
facts: ≈ 230 km · 9–10 h by road, or ≈ 45 min by helicopter
Shiva cave temple, Maratika long-life cave of Guru Rinpoche, Kirat Rai heritage

highlights.title: The main Halesi cave
highlights.text: Steps lead down into a domed cavern with a skylight in the roof, about 60 m across. The natural lingam of Halesi Mahadev sits inside, and priests perform puja through the day. The scale of the chamber surprises most first-time visitors.

highlights.title: Maratika long-life cave
highlights.text: Buddhists revere the caves as the place where Guru Rinpoche and Mandarava attained long-life realisation. Pilgrims crawl through narrow passages and circle the site, and monasteries offer prayers and retreats.

highlights.title: Three faiths at one site
highlights.text: Hindu priests, Buddhist monks and Kirat Rai worshippers all use the caves. On festival days you may see saffron-clad sadhus, maroon-robed monks and Rai elders within a few metres of each other.

highlights.title: Maha Shivaratri mela
highlights.text: On Shivaratri the village fills with pilgrims, sadhus and stalls, and queues for the main cave can stretch for hours. It is the most atmospheric time to visit, and the most crowded.

highlights.title: Monasteries around the caves
highlights.text: Several Tibetan Buddhist monasteries and retreat centres built since the 1980s surround the site. Visitors can usually enter the prayer halls outside ritual times; dress modestly and walk clockwise.

highlights.title: Hill views over Khotang
highlights.text: Mahadevsthan sits on a ridge with views across terraced hills and down to the Dudh Koshi. On clear winter mornings, snow peaks appear on the northern horizon.

how_to_reach.text: From Kathmandu: ≈ 230 km and 9–10 hours via Dhulikhel, the BP Highway through Sindhuli to Khurkot, then Ghurmi and the hill road up to Halesi. Some sections are rough; a private jeep or SUV is better than a car. Buses run daily from Kathmandu.
Charter helicopters from Kathmandu land near Halesi in about 45 minutes, allowing a same-day darshan. Morning flights are the most reliable; cloud often closes routes by afternoon.
Lamidanda airport in Khotang, once used for Halesi, is listed as inactive. Tumlingtar and Biratnagar are the nearest working airports, both several hours away by road.
From the east, Halesi can be reached from Dharan or Biratnagar via the Koshi area and Udayapur hill roads in about 7–9 hours, depending on road conditions. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Mahadevsthan village around the caves has simple hotels and lodges catering to pilgrims, with attached rooms, hot water and vegetarian Nepali and Indian food; they fill quickly around Shivaratri. Some of the Buddhist monasteries have guest rooms intended mainly for retreat participants, and may accept visitors by arrangement. Comfort is basic, with occasional power cuts. If you want more choice, plan a heli day trip from Kathmandu instead. We confirm a recently checked property with your quote.
tips: Wear shoes that grip and clothes you can kneel in: some cave passages are low and slippery.
Carry a small torch for the side caves, which are dimly lit.
Leather items, including belts, are often not allowed inside the main shrine; leave them in the vehicle.
Visit on a weekday outside festival dates for short queues and a calmer darshan.
On the road journey, start from Kathmandu by 6 a.m. to reach Halesi before dark.

experiences.title: Halesi cave darshan with puja
experiences.summary: Enter the main Halesi cave with a local guide, join a puja at the natural Shiva lingam, then visit the smaller caves linked to Parvati and other deities, timed for the quieter early morning hours.
body: We walk from the hotel to the cave entrance at around 6.30 a.m., when the light falls through the opening in the roof and the queue is short. Steps lead down into the domed main chamber. Your guide explains the legends: Shiva hiding from the demon Bhasmasur, who had been granted the power to turn anyone to ash with a touch, and the cave as one of the places where the god escaped.

At the lingam a priest performs a puja for your family, with flowers, milk, bel leaves and a small donation set by the temple. We then visit side caves where shapes in the rock are worshipped as other gods and as Parvati, some reached through narrow, low passages. Those who do not want to squeeze through can wait in the main chamber.
The whole visit takes 2 to 3 hours at a relaxed pace. After darshan there is time for breakfast before continuing to the Buddhist monasteries or starting the drive or flight back.

faqs.q: Is the Halesi cave suitable for elderly people?
faqs.a: The main cave is reached by steps and is manageable for most seniors with a hand to hold. The side caves involve low, narrow passages that can be skipped. Plan extra time and go early to avoid standing in long queues.

faqs.q: Can we take photos inside Halesi cave?
faqs.a: Photography of the main chamber is usually allowed, but not of the lingam during puja or of people praying without permission. Ask your guide or the priests on the day.

faqs.q: What should I offer at Halesi Mahadev?
faqs.a: Typical offerings are flowers, bel leaves, milk, incense, fruits and a donation. Puja sets are sold at stalls near the entrance. There is no fixed amount for the priest; your guide will suggest a fair figure.

experiences.title: Maratika monasteries and long-life cave
experiences.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, any season
experiences.summary: Visit the Tibetan Buddhist monasteries around Halesi and the caves associated with Guru Padmasambhava and Mandarava, learning why Buddhists travel here for long-life practices.
body: In Tibetan Buddhist tradition, Maratika is one of the great pilgrimage places linked to Guru Padmasambhava, also called Guru Rinpoche, who brought tantric Buddhism to Tibet in the 8th century. According to the texts, he and his consort Mandarava meditated here and attained the realisation of long life through the practice of Amitayus, the Buddha of Infinite Life.

Our guide takes you to the cave Buddhists associate with this event and to the main monasteries built around the site since the 1980s. Depending on the day, you may hear monks chanting, see butter lamps being lit or meet pilgrims from Bhutan, Sikkim or further afield on retreat. Visitors are welcome in prayer halls outside ritual times; remove shoes and walk clockwise.

This visit pairs naturally with the Hindu darshan in the main cave and helps explain how the same rock can hold different meanings for different faiths. Donations to the monasteries are appreciated but never required.

faqs.q: Why is Maratika important to Buddhists?
faqs.a: Tibetan Buddhists believe Guru Padmasambhava and Mandarava attained long-life realisation in the Maratika cave. It is visited for long-life blessings and retreats, especially by followers of the Nyingma school.
Yes, outside ritual times. Dress modestly, remove shoes and hats, walk clockwise and ask before photographing monks or shrines.

faqs.q: Is Halesi part of the Buddhist circuit in Nepal?
faqs.a: It is not on the classic Lumbini route, but serious Buddhist pilgrims add it to Kathmandu's Boudhanath, Pharping and Namo Buddha because of its link with Guru Rinpoche.

experiences.title: Rai village and ridge walk at Halesi
experiences.summary: A gentle afternoon walk from Mahadevsthan through Rai farming hamlets and along the ridge for views over the Khotang hills, with an introduction to how the Kirat Rai honour Halesi as an ancestral home.
body: Halesi is not only a temple; it sits in the heart of Rai country. On this walk a local guide takes you out of the pilgrim bazaar and along footpaths through terraced fields of maize, millet and mustard to small Rai hamlets. Houses are built of stone and mud with carved wooden windows, and in the late afternoon you will see families bringing in animals and preparing the evening meal.

Your guide explains how the Kirat Rai trace their ancestry, according to the Mundhum oral tradition, to an ancestor who lived in the Halesi cave, and why the site matters to their identity. If you visit around the full moon of Baisakh or Mangsir, you might see preparations for Sakela, the Rai festival of the farming year, with its circle dances and drums.
The route climbs gently to a ridge viewpoint for sunset over the hills and returns to the village by dusk. It is an easy walk of about 5 km, suitable for most ages.

faqs.q: Why is Halesi important to the Rai people?
faqs.a: According to the Kirat Mundhum, an ancestor of the Rai lived in the Halesi cave, so many Rai regard it as an ancestral place and worship there in their own rites alongside Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims.
No. It is about 5 km on village paths with gentle ups and downs, taking around 3 hours with stops. Wear comfortable shoes.

faqs.q: Can we see Sakela at Halesi?
faqs.a: Sakela is celebrated at the Baisakh full moon (April–May) and the Mangsir full moon (November–December). If your visit falls near those dates, your guide will find out whether a local celebration is happening.

faqs.q: How do I reach Halesi Mahadev from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: By road it is about 230 km and 9–10 hours via Dhulikhel, Sindhuli and Ghurmi, best done in a private jeep. By helicopter it takes about 45 minutes each way, making a same-day darshan possible. Lamidanda airport, once used for Halesi, is listed as inactive.

Our 4-night road yatra from Kathmandu starts from about ₹30,000 per person, twin sharing, with private vehicle, guide and simple hotels. A same-day helicopter yatra starts from about ₹62,000 per seat when five passengers share. Prices depend on group size and season.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Halesi?
faqs.a: October to March gives dry roads and pleasant days. Maha Shivaratri in February or March is the most important festival, with huge crowds. The monsoon from June to September brings landslides on the hill roads.
No. Halesi is not one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of India, but it is one of the most revered Shiva sites in eastern Nepal, sometimes called the Pashupatinath of the east by local pilgrims.

faqs.q: Can I do Halesi in one day by helicopter?
faqs.a: Yes. A morning helicopter from Kathmandu lands near Halesi in about 45 minutes, allows around 1.5–2 hours for darshan and the caves, and returns before noon. Flights depend on weather, so keep the afternoon free in case of delays.

faqs.q: Is Halesi Mahadev the same as Maratika Cave?
faqs.a: Yes, it is the same cave complex. Hindus call it Halesi Mahadev, after Shiva; Tibetan Buddhists call it Maratika, after the cave where Guru Rinpoche attained long-life realisation.
Yes, simple lodges and hotels in Mahadevsthan village serve pilgrims, with vegetarian food and hot water. Some monasteries have retreat rooms. Book early for Shivaratri, when rooms sell out.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Halesi Mahadev?
faqs.a: Hindu legend says Shiva granted the demon Bhasmasur a boon to turn anyone to ash by touching their head. Bhasmasur then chased Shiva, who hid in caves including Halesi until Vishnu tricked the demon into touching his own head.

faqs.q: Is the road to Halesi safe?
faqs.a: In the dry season with an experienced driver, yes. The BP Highway is paved, but the hill section after Ghurmi has narrow and rough stretches. Avoid driving after dark and during heavy monsoon rain.
